By Thomas Novelly · Oct 29, 2026

Happy Thursday, y'all! Welcome back to our weekly space-focused edition of the newsletter.

🛰️ Space domain awareness: Ukraine's Himera and Denmark's GomSpace have launched a test satellite for a future Ukrainian communications network, the firms announced Tuesday.

  • Colin Demarest and I unpack Europe's sovereign SATCOM push below.

🚀 Watch this space: Let's look at Cape Canaveral, China's spaceplane, and orbital food delivery.

Today's newsletter is 1,597 words, a 6-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Cape Canaveral's crescendo
 

A Falcon 9 rocket mission from Space Launch Complex 40 at Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 13. Photo: Gwendolyn Kurzen/DVIDS
 

Call it a new Apollo moment: Rocket launches from Cape Canaveral, Florida, are now outpacing those of the Cold War-era space race that first made the launch site famous.

Why it matters: U.S. leaders are rushing to grow the number of rocket providers at America's busiest spaceport amid a space and arms race with China.

  • Beijing plans to send a crew to the Moon by 2030 or sooner and is rapidly building up its satellite and rocket fleets.

What they're saying: "There's nothing really comparable in the background of my career to what we're experiencing today," Space Force Col. Brian Chatman, the commander of Florida's rocket range, told me in an exclusive interview.

Behind the scenes: The Cape is busy expanding to meet President Trump's mandate for the nation to support 1,000 annual launches by 2030. Chatman said with all the contractors on base, inspection backups and parking chaos abound.

A rundown of some major projects Chatman is overseeing:

  • SpaceX is expanding its footprint on the Cape for its Starship super heavy-lift launchpads.
  • Newcomers Relativity Space and Stoke Space are setting up their facilities and are aiming to launch rockets for military and commercial customers sometime in late 2026 and 2027.
  • NASA is preparing for next year's Artemis III testing missions, and the Artemis IV voyage that aims to return astronauts to the Moon by 2028.
  • Blue Origin is rapidly rebuilding its launch complex after its New Glenn rocket exploded in May.

Jamie Draper, the Cape Canaveral Space Force Museum's director, told me there's been "boom and bust" cycles throughout the base's history.

  • "We're definitely in one of those boom cycles right now," Draper said.

By the numbers: Last year, Space Launch Delta 45, the military command overseeing the Cape, supported 109 orbital liftoffs from the base — the most in its history.

  • In April, Space Launch Delta 45 oversaw five different rocket launches for unique missions, breaking a record set at the height of the U.S.-Soviet space race in the 1960s.
  • Space Force officials estimate that the number of Cape launches could rise from the 109 it reached in 2025 to "approximately 1,200 by 2036" annually, according to the service's vision plan.

Reality check: There's only one other military spaceport in the U.S. — California's Vandenberg Space Force Base — and the two can't fully handle the anticipated surge in commercial and military demand. Top military leaders stress the need for a third U.S. port.

  • Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, the head of Space Systems Command, told reporters last week that another spaceport was likely needed by 2030.

Enter SpaceX: The newly public Elon Musk-controlled company plans to start building another site off the Louisiana coast next year, with its first Starship launch planned for 2029.

  • That site, known as Starbase, would "relieve quite a lot of the pressure" on Cape Canaveral, said Brian Weeden, director of civil and commercial policy for the Aerospace Corporation's Center for Space Policy and Strategy.

The bottom line: Until new spaceports arrive, Cape Canaveral will remain the linchpin of the nation's rocket enterprise.

  • "We have a prime piece of real estate here that maximizes launch opportunities," Chatman said. "But the reality is, there's so much demand for launch in the future that we just need more sites."
 
 
2. DIA's deep dive
 

A photo of China's reusable spaceplane captured in 2024. Photo: Courtesy of Vantor
 

The clearest image to date of China's highly secretive spaceplane was circulated this week in a new Pentagon report identifying space threats.

Why it matters: The photo is further evidence of China's space advancements, and the findings from the Defense Intelligence Agency shine a light on Beijing's orbital arms buildup.

  • The spaceplane photo, taken by space intelligence firm Vantor and shared with Axios, is from May 28, 2024. It shows a satellite docked to the space vehicle and open payload bay doors.
  • The 130-page report points out China's space threats, as well as those from Russia, North Korea and Iran. The release follows the American military's revelation that the U.S. has orbital weapons at the ready.

What they're saying: Despite China's push for non-weaponization agreements, the country is expanding its space tech "to deter and compel other nations from taking actions Beijing deems counter to its national security interests," the DIA wrote.

  • "China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk."
  • Vantor is raising alarm, too.
  • "China is building an unblinking eye over the Pacific, primarily through commercial space capabilities," Will Cocos, executive vice president and general manager of Vantor's U.S. government business, said in an emailed statement. "The DIA's latest report makes clear how quickly that threat is growing."

Threat level: The DIA provided general examples of the space weapons enemies could use on commercial, civil or military satellites, including:

  • radio frequency jammers
  • lasers
  • high-powered microwaves
  • chemical sprayers
  • robotic mechanisms
  • projectiles
  • nuclear detonation

China also has ground-based lasers that can "disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites" in low-Earth orbit, the report said.

  • The country may improve upon that existing technology and could even field space-based lasers "by the late 2020s," according to the DIA.

Yes, but: Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation's chief director of space security and stability, told me DIA has been trying for years to pin a date on when China will field its most advanced laser weapons.

  • "It seems speculative," Samson said.
 
 
3. Elon uncertainty
By Thomas Novelly and Colin Demarest
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

Rival satellite companies are jockeying to loosen Elon Musk's grip on battlefield communications after his company's restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink service shook officials in Europe and the U.S.

Why it matters: The episode, which temporarily disrupted Ukraine's drone usage, shows how vulnerable a military can be to the whims of a single company or market dominator.

State of play: Musk's SpaceX, which is the parent company of Starlink, is by far the world's leader in space-based connectivity with more than 11,000 satellites, per the American Enterprise Institute's data. Eutelsat, a France-based SATCOM firm, is behind them with more than 600 satellites in its OneWeb network.

  • This summer, Starlink announced it hit 12 million customers across more than 160 countries and territories.
  • SpaceX's massive lead has made it difficult for European countries that want to establish independence from the Musk-led company.

Driving the news: Now, non-U.S. firms seeking to compete with SpaceX are pitching their services with more urgency.

  • Last week, Finnish firms ICEYE and Nokia announced an agreement with Ukraine's defense ministry to explore "sovereign satellite communications."
  • The duo's initial satellites are "expected to launch in 2028," an ICEYE spokesperson told Axios, adding the need for reliable satellite communications has been "evident for years, especially in Europe."
  • "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the ICEYE-and-Nokia announcement.
  • "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."

4. Quick hits
 

Cowboy Space debuted its new "Big Iron" rocket design on Oct. 26. Photo: Courtesy of Cowboy Space
 

🚀 California's Vandenberg Space Force Base broke its all-time launch record.

  • The big picture: The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launch on Tuesday marked the 72nd launch that the Space Force supported from the base, according to the service.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: There are still two months left in this year, meaning the West Coast's launch range is heading for never-before-seen heights.

👀 Tim Morrison, a former Boeing defense executive and National Security Council official, has joined Washington Harbour Partners.

  • Follow the money: Washington Harbour, based in Virginia, has backed many well-known defense-tech players, including Apex Space, SpaceX and Turion Space.
  • 💭 Colin's thought bubble: Morrison's warning and rationale are worth a read. Check that out, here.

⛰️ Appalachia and the Midwest want in on the space game, my colleague Ryan Deto reported yesterday.

  • By the numbers: The tri-state region has more than 1,000 space industry firms that have brought in more than $9.5 billion in federal deals over the last four years, according to the Keystone Space Collaborative.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: California, Florida and Texas are the big space hubs, but new initiatives, like Trump's Space Academy, could pull investment away from the coasts.

🇵🇱 Poland will host a new Patriot missile maintenance facility, the Pentagon announced on Tuesday.

  • What they're saying: Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment said NATO is "serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action."
  • 💭 Colin's thought bubble: The new facility is about as close to Russia as you can comfortably get.
 
 
5. Check this out
 

An Air Force Research Laboratory cargo pod for training and exercising recovery operations. Photo: Courtesy of SpaceX/via DVIDS
 

Rocket Door Dash? The Air Force Research Laboratory said it delivered military cargo using a SpaceX Starfall capsule last week.

  • Since 2021, the military has been exploring if cargo aboard a launched rocket can be delivered to a location back on Earth in less than an hour.
  • The pod inside was filled with survival equipment, water and two MREs (meals ready to eat).

Why it matters: Space-based cargo delivery could make dangerous battlefield deliveries safer in the future.

  • AFRL is working with multiple firms including Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space and Outpost Space, according to the press release.

Fun fact: Years ago, I wrote about the South Carolina factory where they make MREs.

  • In my opinion, the Italian sausage with peppers MRE isn't half bad!
